_note: Hand-written beginner targets. Star ids are Hipparcos (HIP) numbers that match stars.json. Facts like distance and brightness are NOT stored here: the app reads them from stars.json so they always come from the catalogue. Planets and the Moon are positioned live by astronomy-engine.

targets.title: The Pole Star
targets.puzzle: Find a medium-bright star in the north that sits on its own. It is the one star that hardly moves all night.
hints: Face north.
Its height above the horizon is about the same as your latitude in degrees.
It is not the brightest star in the sky, just the steadiest.
targets.unlock_fact: Every other star in the northern sky seems to circle around this one during the night.

targets.title: The Summer Triangle
targets.puzzle: Find three bright stars that form a big triangle.
hints: Start with the brightest of the three. It is bluish-white.
The triangle is large: roughly two outstretched hands across.
One corner star is far fainter-looking than its true power, because it is very far away.
targets.unlock_fact: The three corners belong to three different constellations: Lyra, Cygnus and Aquila.

targets.title: Cassiopeia
targets.puzzle: Find five stars making a big letter W (or M, depending on the time).
hints: Look toward the north.
It sits on the opposite side of the Pole Star from the Big Dipper.
The five stars are similar in brightness, none very bright.
targets.unlock_fact: The W flips into an M as the night goes on, because the sky turns around the Pole Star.

targets.title: The Big Dipper
targets.puzzle: Find seven stars shaped like a ladle or a saucepan with a curved handle.
hints: Look toward the north. From India it can sit low or below the horizon at some times of year.
Four stars make the bowl, three make the handle.
The two stars at the outer edge of the bowl point toward the Pole Star.
targets.unlock_fact: These seven stars are only part of a larger constellation, Ursa Major, the Great Bear.

targets.title: The Great Square of Pegasus
targets.puzzle: Find four fairly bright stars forming a large, almost perfect square.
hints: The square is big, so look for it with your whole field of view, not one small patch.
The inside of the square looks nearly empty in a city.
Try counting how many stars you can see inside it. That tells you how dark your sky is.
targets.unlock_fact: One corner star actually belongs to the neighbouring constellation Andromeda.

targets.title: The Pleiades
targets.puzzle: Find a small, tight, fuzzy group of stars that looks like a tiny dipper.
hints: It is much smaller than the Big Dipper. Your thumb held at arm's length almost covers it.
Looking slightly to the side of it often shows more stars than looking straight at it.
Count the stars you can see. Most people see five to seven.
targets.unlock_fact: These stars were born together and are moving through space as one family.

targets.title: Orion's Belt
targets.puzzle: Find three bright stars in a short, nearly straight line, evenly spaced.
hints: They are close together: the whole line is less than two fingers wide at arm's length.
A reddish bright star sits above them and a bluish one below.
In October they rise late at night. Check the app's 'best time' first.
targets.unlock_fact: The three belt stars look side by side, but they are at very different distances from us.

targets.title: Sirius
targets.puzzle: Follow the line of Orion's Belt downward until you hit the brightest star in the night sky.
hints: Extend the belt line to the lower left (in the northern hemisphere).
Near the horizon it often twinkles in different colours.
targets.unlock_fact: It looks the brightest partly because it is one of the nearest stars to us.

targets.title: Antares
targets.puzzle: Find a bright reddish-orange star low in the sky, in the middle of a curving line of stars.
hints: Its colour is the giveaway: clearly orange-red next to white stars.
It is the heart of Scorpius, the scorpion.
targets.unlock_fact: Its name roughly means 'rival of Mars', because of its red colour.

targets.title: Tonight's planet
targets.puzzle: Find a bright 'star' that does not twinkle much.
hints: Planets usually shine with a steadier light than stars.
They always lie near the same band across the sky that the Sun and Moon follow.
targets.unlock_fact: Unlike stars, planets shift their position against the background stars from week to week.

targets.title: The Moon
targets.puzzle: Find the Moon and note its shape.
hints: The app tells you its phase and whether it is up right now.
targets.unlock_fact: A bright Moon washes out faint stars, so moonless nights are best for hard challenges.
